result: ACE-2 is the receptor for both SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2, enabling viral entry into cells.
evaluation: Claims C1, C15, and C56 consistently establish ACE-2 as the receptor for both SARS-CoV (known since 2005) and SARS-CoV-2 (identified in 2020). This is well-supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge in the field.

result: SARS-CoV-2 shares structural similarity with SARS-CoV, including 76.5% homology in spike protein sequence and nearly identical receptor binding domain structure, but binds ACE-2 with higher affinity, potentially explaining its virulence and lung tropism.
evaluation: Claims C13, C18-C20 provide quantitative structural data from cited sources. Claims C21-C22 offer reasonable mechanistic speculation based on the binding affinity data. The structural similarity is well-documented, though the causal link to virulence (C21-C22) remains somewhat speculative.

result: ACE-2 is highly expressed in vascular endothelium and lung tissue, particularly in endothelial and type 2 alveolar epithelial cells, with preferential apical localization. ACE-2 shares only 42% sequence homology with ACE-1.
evaluation: Claims C16-C17, C24, C44-C45 are well-supported by multiple citations describing ACE-2 tissue distribution and structural characteristics. The expression patterns and sequence homology data are established facts from the cited literature.

result: SARS-CoV-2 enters cells by binding ACE-2, activating TMPRSS2, and fusing with the cell membrane. Viral entry can be prevented by neutralizing antibodies or TMPRSS2 inhibitors (camostat, nafamostat mesylate).
evaluation: Claims C23, C25-C28 describe the viral entry mechanism with appropriate citations. Claims C29-C30 provide regulatory context for potential therapeutics. The mechanistic description is well-established and supported by cited experimental evidence.

result: ACE-1 cleaves angiotensin I to generate angiotensin II, which causes vasoconstriction, bronchoconstriction, increased vascular permeability, inflammation, and fibrosis, thereby promoting ARDS and lung failure in SARS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2 infections.
evaluation: Claims C31-C37 describe established biochemistry of the ACE-1/Ang II pathway. Claims C38-C41 extend this to SARS-CoV/SARS-CoV-2 pathology with citation support (Yang et al., 2015). The mechanistic chain from Ang II effects to ARDS is well-documented in the cited literature.

result: ACE-2 cleaves angiotensin I and II to generate Ang(1-9) and Ang(1-7), which activate protective pathways (ACE-2–Ang(1-7)–AT2R and ACE-2–Ang(1-7)–MasR) with vasodilatory, anti-inflammatory, anti-proliferative, and antifibrotic effects that counterbalance the harmful ACE-1–Ang II–AT1R pathway.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 and C89-C97 describe the protective arm of the renin-angiotensin system. These are presented as established knowledge with implicit citation support. The biochemical mechanisms and physiological effects are well-documented in the cardiovascular literature.

result: The ACE-1–Ang II–AT1R pathway contributes to ARDS pathophysiology, while activation of ACE-2–Ang(1-7)–AT2R and ACE-2–Ang(1-7)–MasR pathways is protective. Experimental evidence shows ACE-2 deletion worsens ARDS, while Ang(1-7), ACEIs, and ARBs improve it, indicating ACE-2 activation limits disease progression.
evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C42-C43, C49-C52, C87-C88, C98-C103 present a coherent body of experimental evidence from animal models. Multiple citations support the protective effects of ACEIs/ARBs and the detrimental effects of ACE-2 deletion. The experimental data consistently support the proposed mechanisms.

result: Imbalance between the ACE-1–Ang II–AT1R pathway and the protective ACE-2-dependent pathways contributes to ARDS and acute lung failure pathogenesis, likely relevant for COVID-19 patients. Blunting the AT1R axis while enhancing protective axes likely protects from ARDS triggered by infectious pathogens including coronaviruses.
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 and C144-C150 synthesize prior experimental evidence into a mechanistic framework. While the extension to COVID-19 (C150) involves some speculation, it is a reasonable inference based on SARS-CoV data and the shared ACE-2 receptor mechanism. The underlying pathway imbalance concept is well-supported by cited studies.

result: Early commentaries suggested ACEIs/ARBs might be harmful in COVID-19 by increasing ACE-2 levels, but the authors found no supporting evidence for ACE-2 upregulation by these drugs in the lungs. Evidence of ACE-2 upregulation applies to cardiac tissue as a compensatory response to underlying conditions, not drug treatment.
evaluation: Claims C57-C65 critically evaluate prior hypotheses. The authors document that cited sources (C62) did not support the claimed mechanism and that their literature search (C63) found no supporting data. Claims C64-C65 provide alternative explanations for observed ACE-2 upregulation with appropriate citations. This represents a valid critical assessment of the literature.

result: Increased plasma ACE-2 levels can capture the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 and SARS-CoV in plasma, preventing viral binding to lung cells. This strategy has been suggested to protect against SARS-CoV-2 lung infection.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 present a mechanistic rationale for soluble ACE-2 therapy with citation support (Kruse, 2020; Zhang et al., 2020). The mechanism is biologically plausible based on receptor-ligand interactions, though C66-C67 involve some inference about the protective mechanism.

result: Administering recombinant soluble ACE-2 could capture and inactivate SARS-CoV-2 in plasma, prevent viral binding to lung cells, and enhance ACE-2 activity in lung tissue. This represents a potential therapeutic strategy for COVID-19 patients with ARDS, possibly even at late stages requiring mechanical ventilation.
evaluation: Claims C5, C116-C119, C129-C131 propose a therapeutic strategy based on mechanistic reasoning. While the underlying mechanism is plausible (supported by C66-C69), these claims are explicitly speculative proposals without direct experimental validation in COVID-19 patients. The strategy requires clinical testing to confirm efficacy and safety.

result: A 2017 pilot trial in ARDS patients showed that rhACE-2 increased Ang(1-7) and surfactant protein D levels and tended to lower IL-6 concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C120-C123 report findings from a cited pilot trial (Khan et al., 2017). The results are presented accurately with appropriate qualification ("tended to lower" for IL-6). This provides some preliminary evidence supporting the rhACE-2 therapeutic strategy, though the trial was not in COVID-19 patients.

result: SARS-CoV-2 infection downregulates ACE-2 expression in endothelial and type 2 alveolar epithelial cells, thereby downregulating the protective ACE-2–Ang(1-7)–MasR pathway and leaving lungs exposed and unprotected from detrimental Ang II effects via AT1R.
evaluation: Claims C109-C111 describe ACE-2 downregulation with citations (Kuba et al., 2005; Imai et al., 2008). Claims C126-C128 extend this to the mechanistic consequences. The downregulation is documented, and the inference about loss of protective effects (C127-C128) follows logically from the established pathway biology.

result: ACEIs and ARBs can be beneficial in SARS-CoV-2 infection by blunting the ACE-1–Ang II–AT1R pathway, counterbalancing ACE-2 downregulation, and rescuing the downregulated protective pathways in the lungs.
evaluation: Claims C112-C115 and C141-C143 present mechanistic inferences about ACEI/ARB benefits in COVID-19. While the underlying pathway biology is well-established, the specific application to COVID-19 involves extrapolation from animal models and SARS-CoV data. Direct clinical evidence in COVID-19 patients is not provided, making this inference reasonable but requiring validation.

result: In meta-analyses and case-control studies involving over 21,000 patients across multiple high-risk populations (stroke survivors, Asian populations, Parkinson's disease patients), ACEIs were superior to other antihypertensive agents in pneumonia prevention.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 report findings from large-scale studies with appropriate citations. The evidence spans multiple patient populations and study designs, providing robust support for ACEI benefits in pneumonia prevention. This represents established clinical evidence, though not specific to COVID-19.

result: Experimental data for SARS-CoV show that ACEIs and ARBs can be protective rather than harmful, leading to proposals for enhancing the protective arm of the renin-angiotensin system as a therapeutic strategy for pulmonary diseases.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 summarize experimental findings with citation (Tan et al., 2018). The protective effects in SARS-CoV models provide relevant precedent for SARS-CoV-2, given the viruses' similarities. The therapeutic strategy proposal is a reasonable extension of the experimental evidence.

result: Abrupt withdrawal of RAAS inhibitors in high-risk patients (stage 3 hypertension, heart failure, post-MI) may result in clinical instability and adverse health outcomes.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86 cite established cardiovascular medicine principles (Vaduganathan et al., 2020). The risks of abrupt RAAS inhibitor withdrawal in high-risk cardiovascular patients are well-documented. This provides important clinical context for the discontinuation debate.

result: Multiple scientific societies (ESH, Italian Society of Cardiology, Italian Society of Arterial Hypertension, HFSA/ACC/AHA, European Medicines Agency) and medical journal editors released statements affirming there is no evidence that ACEIs and ARBs jeopardize COVID-19 patients or support discontinuing treatment.
evaluation: Claims C70-C72 and C75-C77 document official positions from major medical organizations. These statements represent expert consensus based on available evidence at the time. The authors accurately report these institutional positions with appropriate citations.

result: ACEIs and ARBs provide cardiovascular, renal, and pulmonary protection in SARS-CoV-2-associated ARDS and are unlikely to be detrimental—likely protective—in COVID-19 patients. Rebalancing the renin-angiotensin system using ACEIs/ARBs while enhancing the ACE-2 axis is a valuable strategy to minimize SARS-CoV-2 harm to the lungs.
evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C104-C107, and C151 represent the authors' main therapeutic conclusions. While mechanistically sound based on pathway biology and animal models, these claims involve significant extrapolation to COVID-19 patients. The protective effects are inferred from indirect evidence rather than direct COVID-19 clinical trials. The conclusions are reasonable but require prospective clinical validation.

result: In cardiovascular disease patients on ACEIs/ARBs who are at risk of or infected with SARS-CoV-2 (but not requiring mechanical ventilation), there is no evidence for deleterious effects of these medications. Discontinuing these life-saving medications may be harmful.
evaluation: Claims C9, C152-C154 present clinical recommendations. While C152-C153 correctly note the absence of evidence for harm, the positive assertion that discontinuation "may be harmful" (C9, C154) involves inference from withdrawal risks in cardiovascular patients and mechanistic reasoning. The recommendation is clinically prudent but not directly proven in COVID-19 populations at the time of writing.

result: Whether mineralocorticoid receptor blockers are protective in COVID-19 remains unknown.
evaluation: Claim C108 appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about mineralocorticoid receptor blockers. This represents an honest assessment of knowledge gaps and avoids overextending conclusions beyond available evidence.

result: As of April 2, 2020, SARS-CoV-2 had infected one million and killed more than 50,000 people worldwide, with an estimated 79% infection rate from undocumented cases. Italy had the highest number of cases in the EU and deaths worldwide at the manuscript date.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 and C73-C74 report epidemiological data with appropriate temporal context. These represent factual data points from the early pandemic period, accurately cited and temporally qualified.

result: SARS-CoV was responsible for a global outbreak that killed 774 people in 2003.
evaluation: Claim C14 reports historical epidemiological data about the 2003 SARS outbreak. This is well-established historical fact with appropriate citation.

result: Type 2 alveolar epithelial cells are equipped with molecular machinery allowing rapid viral replication, thus enhancing pulmonary spreading of infection.
evaluation: Claims C124-C125 describe cellular characteristics relevant to viral pathogenesis. This represents established knowledge about type 2 alveolar epithelial cells' role in viral replication, presented in the figure caption.

result: Ang II promotes inflammation, vasoconstriction, cell proliferation, vascular leakage, and pulmonary fibrosis via AT1R. These effects are counteracted by ACE-2-dependent formation of Ang(1-7) and Ang(1-9) activating AT2R, MasR, and MrgD receptors.
evaluation: Claims C132-C140 summarize established renin-angiotensin system biology presented in the figure. These represent well-documented physiological mechanisms with extensive literature support, appropriately synthesized in the figure caption.
